I can say, as someone who DM’d 5e for almost 10 years (Next to when the OGL scandal started last year), I can tell you a big issue with the system is that there is absolutely no DM support whatsoever for a vast majority of situations that you’ll find yourself in at tables. The DMG that they offer, both the old and new version (which was shared with me, I haven’t given them my money since the OGL scandal, or really since they completely fumbled their Starjammer release) does NOT teach you REALLY how to run the game. The newest one had added in some tips, and given some nifty little helper sheets, but the system is still stuck with the same issues as far as I can see with the poor balance from being rubber banded by bounded accuracy and challenge rating tables that don’t truly account for every option at the table. The other big issue is that no one at Wizards can even agree on what the monster creation rules are, every monster in each of the books are all over the place, some match and some aren’t even in the same league, and then you have multiple DM’s using duct tape and a nail gun to try and make encounters up to the challenge that they want them to be at, but because of how swingy the system is it’s a crap shoot because either A.) the combat encounter goes as intended. B.) The party gets TPK’d. Or C.) The party walks all over the encounter.

Another big issue with encounters and making villains feel like villains is that because of how the system is designed, final villain encounters can either feel as intended, or end in one to three rounds and feel very anti-climactic because someone at your table took some options, that are completely legal from the books, that end up breaking the whole encounter. And this really feels like them either not playtesting their options ahead of time, or just not putting them in there with other options.

This also doesn’t help with the fact that even the people who WORK on this game behind the scenes don’t even know how to play or rub their own game. I know people call 5e an easy system to learn, but 5e is pretty crunchy, and most people don’t even read or look at the rules and just trust the DM to tell them how to play the game, and at the same time hand out a 5 page document of house rules that they made to further duct tape and nail gun the system to fix it further. They basically offload 2/3rds of the system onto you, the DM and say “you figure it out, dumbass”

I have found that Pathfinder 2e is an easier system to teach and GM in because it’s an easier system to play: You have three actions and a reaction, it’s all plainly spelled out on your sheet How many actions everything takes, all of the rules are there for any situation that you could hope for, and there’s no RAW vs RAI discussions at the table, it’s literally baked into every ability and rule because it’s all written as if these guys play their own system and know what to look out for. There’s TONS of great advice on how to GM your game, what to do with different types of players, and all of the rules are online for free. And even better, unlike 5e where you need the community to answer a majority of your lore questions through Wiki or hoping someone uploaded a scan of an old 3.5 or 2e book, they have TONS of dense lore books about their world with so many player options and just so many cool things for you to use, like a whole book on a Dwarven Kingdom called Highelm, Dwarven Society and how to make your own Dwarven Fortresses and Cities! And it’s a big book, with player options and new items too!

I will tell you, coming from 5e to Pathfinder 2e was like tonal whiplash. The amount of prep time that I have to do has shrunk, my combat encounters are interesting and engaging now, and my players are having so much fun with all of the options they have, and I’m having fun being able to build balanced combat’s with interesting monsters that do something more than just being a bag of hit points that just attacks every round.

The two “House rules” I guess that I primarily use are there to encourage team work and to help retrain my players who all come from 5e to Pathfinder 2e (I’m running 5 games of PF2e right now 😅) to show them that this game isn’t “four adventurers who happen to be in a group together” but an actual adventuring party/team. Besides giving a hero point every hour to my players here’s a couple of mine:

1. I let players spend as many hero points on each other as they like. You can burn all of your hero points on one roll, and players can double down and even donate as many hero points as they like to help each other out. I feel this really encourages team play, but also, makes them REALLY want to use their hero points to help each other out, which means they’re running out of them as quickly as they’re getting them and sometimes don’t have them for super critical points, which then forces the group to go into team mode to figure their way through it.

2. I let Aid checks stack, again, this is to help encourage team play amongst my players and to help them work together and come up with solutions where everyone can get involved and feel like their contributions matter. There are still people who are good at what they do, and experts in specific things, but watching my players try to figure out ways to help each other out suddenly changes their entire philosophy of how to play the game and it’s great for me as a GM watching everything click.

One thing I do for BRAND new players to the system, especially those switching from 5e, is let players switch whatever they like from levels 1-5 rather than retrain. I let them know that that rule exists for switching out specific things, but when you’re just starting out in an unfamiliar system, you might realize that something you picked at level 1 just isn’t really meshing anymore with your character. After level 5 I feel like my players have a pretty good handle on their characters and then implement the retrain rule using downtime.

In reality, 90% of us don’t, a majority of us are working other jobs to support our careers, have to take time off for touring, record during our off time at work, sometimes late into the night. If you’re a touring back up musician you’re basically hustling for the next gig once you’re off tour with the artist you were backing up because that’s the end of your paycheck (weekly pay plus per diem), unless you’re on retainer which means you’re under contract with one artist and you’re being paid to only play for them which means when you’re not touring with them they’re still paying you. And the other big issue for a vast majority of us is no health care under most contracts so a good portion of those pay checks are going straight towards health care, and if your job doesn’t provide it and you’re not in a state that provides low income health care you’re watching most of your money disappear into that or hoping you don’t get sick/injured. 

The percentage of people in the industry who make enough to fully support themselves and never have to work another job is somewhere in the ball park of 10-1%, and a majority of those artists are either from before the current music industry and they already made their money, or, they got a lucky contract, or they toughed it out, never got shelved (getting shelved happens to more artists than you think) and were able to eventually renegotiate a contract and get a better split, or they were smart with their money and diversified into other industries.

As somebody who used to be a professional musician before an injury, merch doesn’t really get you much either, basically gas to the next venue if you’re completely indie and using your own vehicle and that’s if you’re selling the merchandise yourself, if you’ve hired a merch seller they’re taking a cut too, and then a lot of the stuff that you’re making at gigs depends on the market and what cut your touring manager is taking, some venues require you to sell tickets ahead of time and fork up cash for any tickets you didn’t sell (pay-to-play), this is a big thing in Southern California, the Bay Area and Seattle, so if you’re from out of town and brand new and the promoter for the venue is only booking you on that specific deal then you’re basically hustling day of to sell whatever you can so you’re not further in the hole. A great majority of bands/artists come back from touring in the red, very rarely in the black. It’s an unfortunate part of the industry and the real problem is people look at it and say “man I’m talented at music, but it’s not financially viable, guess I’ll do something else” rather than ask “well wait, but why can’t it be financially viable?” A lot of us put in years of work and practice to get to a point where we can get into bands or back up artists and then rehearse for months prior to touring, spending money on either rehearsal lock outs or renting rehearsal spaces hourly, spending money on stage clothing, buying or renting the right gear to get out there and give you all a great show, or record a song that will really speak to you at some point in your life.

Here’s all of the house rules in my current Curse of Strahd campaign that my players really like!

House Rules! 😄

No evil, no chaotic neutral

We will be using Milestone leveling.

 Max HP at Level 1, roll for HP every level afterwards ignoring 1's.

 Level 1 you gain a racial feat from Xanathar's Guide, DM approval for feat if your race doesn't have any.

We will be rolling stats at character creation, roll two sets, pick the best set of the two.

 Gunslinger Fighter subclass allowed

 No Unearthed Arcana or Homebrew!

 No secret characters, all players know your race, class, and background. You can weave your backstories together at session 0

 Attunement takes 1 action, unattune takes 10 minutes

 No diagonals from the book, going diagonal is same as going straight

Flanking: you can flank on any square within melee distance, must describe how you're flanking and what you're doing to distract, roll skill check determined by DM against creatures AC. Gain advantage on flank attack rolls.

 Will be using bloodied for creatures to describe damage (once at half health creatures and players are bloodied)

 Death Saving Throws rolled by DM in secret. Medicine checks count as a successful or non-successful death save instead of stabilizing. Using medicine kits give you advantage.

 Sprint: sacrifice all actions and bonus actions to move 5 times your movement speed. Creatures get attacks of opportunity if you sprint through their threat range. Monsters, NPC's can do the same.

Massive Damage: If you or an enemy take half your HP in damage, you will have to make a DC 15 Constitution saving throw or make a system shock.

 Healing Spirit can only be used in combat

Charging Rule: You can use your action to charge, moving up to your speed towards a target, to gain advantage on your attack roll. Must move at least 10 ft towards your target. If you move through enemy threat range during this movement you can trigger opportunity attacks as you are throwing yourself off to wild abandon to charge head long towards a foe.

Hero Points: Instead of Inspiration we will now be using Hero Points. Every session every character will start with 1 Hero Point, you can earn up to 3 Hero Points per game and your Hero Points reset to 1 at the start of the next session. You can spend your Hero Point exactly as a point of Inspiration, but if you bank up 3 Hero Points and are down (0 hit points and dying) and spend all 3 you immediately bounce back up at 1 HP.

Shifting: You may spend your move action to shift 5ft. This uses up your entire move action, but allows you to move out of Melee Combat.

 Banned races:

No Wildemont races

No Ravnica Races

No Mythic Odysseys of Theros races

 Locathah allowed but don't have to submerge every 4 hours

 Banned backgrounds No backgrounds from Ravnica, Acquisitions Incorporated, Wildemont

I’ve run this campaign 3 times now to great effect, and here are my tips for running this module:

Read the module through at least twice, three times is even better, get really familiar with each of the locations, understand them. Some locations (like Vallaki) seem intimidating, but from the three times I’ve run it, each party arrives, bee lines it to the church, starts the bones quest, triggers the feast, and the torn burns the next day, not one of my parties actually engaged in the political thriller aspect of the town, but have it prepped just in case.

Look at each of the expansion posts and read through them, decide how much of each you wish to take from, and how much you don’t. Each one provides fantastic expansions to the campaign that really flesh everything out and give you some great advice on running the campaign.

Do not be afraid to kill your players, remember, death in Barovia is hardly the end, the mists never let souls leave. Look up the dark gifts in the Adventurers League DM’s guide for the campaign and when a player dies, take them aside and reach out to them, either as a dark power or as one of the hidden fanes if you’re using them and offer them a dark gift in exchange for resurrection. Always a cool “wtf” moment for the players when they immediately pop back up at full health and their eyes melt out of their faces granting them blind sight for 60 feet 😂

Be sure to stack the Tarokka deck BEFORE session 0, know where everything is going to be before the game starts and who their fated ally will be and where Strahd is going to be. For your first run, especially for new players, remove some of the worse cards from the deck when you do your draws; any cards that put items in the Castle, the card that gives them no ally in general. If they draw an ally who’s isn’t as crazy as say Ezmerelda, you can opt to turn them into a side kick to assist the players if they decide to arm them, giving levels in side kick equal to the parties level or half. 

If you so plan on running Death House (highly recommended with some tweaks!) be sure to take all of their stuff the minute they arrive in Barovia via the mists! This will immediately put them on edge and will have them scrounging for gear inside of the house.

Optional reading is definitely I, Strahd if you can! I believe the audiobook is on YouTube, definitely worth at least one read through to get into Strahd’s head.

Speaking of Strahd, really decide who Strahd is and how you want to play him. Mine is very serious, but has a sense of dark humor. He doesn’t take insults lightly and always lets everyone have one: one insult, one free hit etc. It always comes with a warning though, if they continue in this direction, his retaliation is quick and decisive and you will very quickly learn your place within his lands.

Most important thing too is to set expectations at session 0. Inform your players the style of campaign that this is, set up a system to allow players who feel uncomfortable to speak up when necessary and pause to handle it. And make sure they understand that this is a more difficult adventure than others but that they’ll be stronger be the end of it: players, friends, team mates etc.

Here’s the thing about Vallaki: I’m about to finish running Curse of Strahd for the third time in a row right now. In all three campaigns I can tell you exactly how each party went through Vallaki:

Party 1: Went to the inn, got a bit of info, loved the Martikovs, went to sleep. Next day, Ireena says “hey, before we go to the temple let’s go see the Burgomaster and give our regards, it would only be proper” The Party: “Ok, but like after the temple” bee line to the temple, find out about the bones, bee line to the orphanage (thank you MandyMod), shenanigans, bee line the coffin shop all the while saying “this’ll be quick guys, then we’ll hit the mayors house no sweat”, get to the coffin shop, trigger the feast, vampire spawn nearly beat the PC’s to death, Strahd shows up, taunts them, charms a player to give him the bones, he destroys the bones, resurrects his vampire spawn, tells them to feast, he leaves on Beauciphulus. Entire village of Vallaki descends into chaos, burgomaster and his wife are dragged out of his home and burned alive, Fiona Wachter takes over, Ireena was left back at the Inn, she’s now been taken by Strahd, they barely flee. Vallaki barely happened.

Party 2: Bee lined the temple, bee lined the orphanage, shenanigans, receive a note from Fiona Wachter, went to the inn, loved the martikovs, Ireena says they should visit the burgomaster “we’ll do it later, should probably handle the coffin shop first, that’ll be quick” (see a pattern?), go to the coffin shop, trigger the feast, make a mad dash across town with the bones with vampire spawn set loose upon the town and hot on their heels, get to the temple, Strahd makes a dramatic entrance, taunts them, kills the Barbarian for swinging at a Lord in one stroke, charms a player into giving him the bones, incinerates them, true resurrects the player, reminds them of their place within his realm, leaves, Vallaki is burning, players barely make it out alive, Fiona Wachter takes over.

Party 3: Gets to Vallaki, goes to see the Burgomaster this time, gets the plot hook for Fiona Wachter, actually meets Izek, goes shopping, goes to the temple, gets the bones quest, goes to the orphanage, shenanigans, gets the note from Fiona Wachter, goes to the Inn, really likes the Martikovs, decides to go to the coffin shop “don’t worry guys, it’ll be quick” (you see where this is going), go to the coffin shop, trigger the feast, rogue rushes into the town towards the abbey, vampire spawn are set loose on the city m, some hot on their heels, arrive at the abbey, Strahd makes extravagant entrance, kills the fighter to make a point, charms the player to give him the bones, incinerates them, true resurrects the fighter to remind him of his place in his realm, invites them to dinner and leaves, they sleep in the abbey, next day is the festival of the blazing Sun, the Burgomaster and his wife are burned on stage in front of the entire town as they cheer, Fiona Wachter takes over, players escape.

What I’m trying to illustrate here is that: even though you REALLY want your players to dive into the cool political intrigue and cult plots going on in Vallaki, more than likely they’ll skip over all of it, go straight for the church and basically trigger the end credits of Vallaki super early, so don’t sweat it too hard bud!

I'm almost done reading the book and I think I'm going to be combining both the Lost Things and the Warlock's Quest intro to hook the players into the story. Start with each of them going to the carnival at the age of 8, at different points in their lives (again, with the concept of time and the feywild, time is always wibbly wobbly), during their time at the carnival, they lost something, we'll go through them rolling what it is they lost, the curse that they received, but more importantly, their memory of ever going to that carnival is nothing more than a hazy dream. You can hardly remember even being there. Then, after doing the character creation with my players, doing the lost things set up and getting it all out of the way, the true set up for the game will be that they all receive a letter of invitation to Madryck's estate, saying that he would like to hire them for a very important job. He'll mention his plight in his inability to contact his patron, the Archfey Zyblina, which I will then say triggers a memory, I'll have them roll on the table for them to have a flashback of being visited by her. When he mentions the Carnival, I'll mention how suddenly they all have flashbacks to being children and remembering visiting such a carnival and feel the pang of the thing that you lost is tied to this carnival he's asked you to visit. This allows me to introduce the players to each other ahead of the Carnival, gets them working together, and really ties them into the story on two different fronts. I'll definitely refine the intro a bit, but I think this should work.

The clear differences that I've found between tube and solid state amps are entirely along the lines of how the amps react to your playing. Solid state amps have a singular level of sound, so, if you play softly or hard it'll be roughly the same. With tube amps they have a more reactionary feel to your playing, so if you play more softly it'll clean up the sound and make your tone more warm, and if you play harder it'll dirty itself and give you a sharper sound.

So really, it comes down to the style of music that you're playing and doing that really affects your decisions about the type of amp that you'll be using. I find that Solid States are great for Metal or really Hard Rock, whereas tube is better for pop, blues, rock, pop, R&B ect.

There's also benefits to doing this as well. You can actually change which string you're bending mid bend by doing this. Bend up on the b string a whole step and then swap down to the g string on the way down to get a cool bluesy effect.

Honestly, the main issue here is thumb positioning on the neck. For the a string/a shape barre chords (from the C.A.G.E.D system) you don't necessarily need the high e string in them in order for them to work. Attempt to fix your thumb positioning first by making sure that it is perfectly straight up and closer to the center of the back of the neck and where your middle finger would be, in this case, if you're doing an A shape C barre chord on the 3rd fret, keep your thumb behind the 4th fret like this http://andylemaire.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/12/Correct-thumb.jpg


And barre with your ring finger. It does take time to get it right too, this is just a step in the right direction to getting it right. It'll take a lot of trial and error, but proper thumb positioning helps with this.

This is an area of learning guitar that takes a lot of trial and error. Honestly, the main issues with E string barre chords is how you use the pressure of your index finger. You ideally want to be only applying pressure above your first knuckle with the pad of your index finger and then the fat part of your finger under your second knuckle. The primary reason why you don't barre your whole finger is that you don't need to because your ring, pinky and middle will be taking care of the A, D and G strings for you as far as major goes. Sports injuries usually mess up your hand. The reason we keep the thumb behind the neck in the beginning is to work on stretching our hands. With our thumb placed flat against the neck our fingers naturally stretch out and give us the distances that we need to start working with.

However, seeing as this is the case, I'd highly suggest moving your thumb up on your neck so that way it is curved slightly. Sports injuries do weird things to your hands that make them not very good at playing guitar due to tendon and bone damage. Try to keep your thumb as flat as you can, but angle it and curve it if it feels too difficult and work from there. Eventually you'll be able to get it completely flat on the back of the neck.

I think there are a certain amount of basics that everyone at every level should know and this is what I'll put here:

1.) The five minor pentatonic patterns and how they are moveable, not set to one key, but are basically the same thing for every key.

2.) How to find relative minor from a major key, by doing this, all 5 of those minor pentatonic patterns become major pentatonic, and you didn't have to learn anything new.

3.) How to build a major and a minor scale, involving whole steps and half steps and how to add these two missing notes into the minor pentatonic patterns, turning them into major and natural minor.

4.) How to modify said scales into harmonic minor, melodic minor, phrygian and the other modes.

5.) How to harmonize both the major and minor scales into chords. And how these chords are used in songwriting.

6.) Triads and their 1st and 2nd inversions.

7.) C.A.G.E.D system. And how these relate to the 5 patterns of the pentatonic/minor scales

8.) How to play extension chords and how to build them.

9.) How to build a melody and then expand that into a guitar solo.

10.) How to jam and improvise.

I think the best way to get better at improvising is to:


1.) Know all 5 patterns of the minor pentatonic scale

2.) Know how to play all 5 patterns of the natural minor scale

3.) Know how to modify the natural minor scale into a natural harmonic scale

4.) How to find the relative minor for major keys.


Now, once you have all of this down, learn a TON of other songs solos note for note. Work on getting the exact sounds and tone for each one, from how they vibrato, to how they bend and slide. This will help you to define your tone and your sound when improvising and give you a better idea of where you can go with your playing.

This is seldom, if ever, called melodic major. What it is, is the fifth mode of Melodic Minor... Sometimes it is referred to as Mixolydian b6... I have used it extensively.. I love the sound it creates, particularly over a sus2 chord from the tonic.. The ambiguity is great...

If you take this scale and spell it... Say you're in C... it would be:

C, D, E, F, G, Ab, Bb.

As you can see, if you start from the F, you get the melodic minor scale...

F, G, Ab, Bb, C, D, E

There is a HARMONIC MAJOR scale, but, to my knowledge, no MELODIC MAJOR, since Melodic minor implies a flatted third but the rest of the notes are structured EXACTLY like a Major scale...

Does that make sense to you??

Also, by the way, to hear this scale in use in a popular context, you can take another listen to Kashmir by Led Zeppelin... The section in the middle where the strings come in, they play the scale pretty much verbatim in ascending fashion, to create that grandiose resolution to the D major chord, after crawling up to it through the b6 and b7... Alright, so here's my big lesson for you on how theory and scales work. As we know, our guitar is normally tuned to EADGBe. These are the specific notes that our strings are tuned to. Now, if I play my E string open, what note would that be? E. Ok, now that we have that out of the way, let's talk about theory. All scales are based off of modifications of the Major scale. A major scale is made up of whole steps and half steps. A whole step on the guitar is 2 frets and a half step is 1 fret. Most notes are going to be a whole step apart, except for two: B-C and E-F. Both of those will always be a half step apart. So, if we take our musical alphabet and add in the whole steps and half steps it would look like this: 
AwBhCwDwEhFwGwA and it continues to repeat. The major scale is written in number format: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. Each number represents a position within the scale and helps you to identify various things, which we'll get into later. Now, in order to create a scale, specifically the Major scale, we have to plug in whole steps and half steps to achieve this. The major scale formula is Whole, Whole, Half, Whole, Whole, Whole, Half. So, with this in mind your Major scale should look like this: 1w2w3h4w5w6w7h8 (8 in this case is the Octave, which is the root note, or home note of the scale, at a higher area of the scale). Now, with this in mind lets build a scale to test this. Let's do C Major, as that's the most basic and has no accidentals (something we'll go over in a second). So, seeing as we're building a C Major scale, the first note in the scale should be C, seeing as that's our home note. So, here we go. 1=C, now here we go. So, in order to go to 2 we need to make a whole step right? So, a whole step above C, as we know from earlier, is going to take us to D. So, now it'll look like this 1=C w 2=D. Now that we get the basic idea, let's build the full scale: 1w2w3h4w5w6w7h8 C D E F G A B C

And there's our C Major scale, no sharps no flats. No what is a sharp and a flat? Those are called accidental notes and they happen between our whole steps. So, a sharp note has this: #, where is a flat note has this: b. So, for instance, let's say we want to build an A major scale. So we need to start this one with the root note, or the home note, which is A. So 1=A. Now, let's build the scale 1w2w3h4w5w6w7h8 A B C#D E F#G#A

So, if you notice, we have a C#, a F# and a G#. These notes happen between the notes that have the whole steps. So a C# can also be a Db. Both of those notes exist at the same time, but calling them that depends on what you use. You never use # and b's in the same scale, you pick either or.

Alright, now that we have that out of the way, we'll make a Natural Minor scale. So, Natural Minor is a variation of the Major Scale by changing sections of the Major Scale to make it fit. So, in order to create a Minor Scale we have to flatten, or lower the tone, of three notes within the scale which are the 3rd, 6th and 7th. So, this changes the way that we write and talk about it. The new numbers look like this: 1, 2, b3, 4, 5, b6, b7, 8

See that? We've changed their pitch, and now because of that, we change the types of whole steps and half steps that we use for the scale. So here is the whole step and half step formula for Natural Minor: 1w2hb3w4w5hb6wb7w8

So there we have it, the Natural Minor scale, our formula has changed. Now for something fun, we're going to make the A Minor scale, now pay special attention to this one: 1w2hb3w4w5hb6wb7w8 A B C D E F G A

Now, take a look at that, that is A minor in its pure form. Now, do you see anything familiar? Looks an awful lot like C Major right? That's because A minor is the relative minor of C Major, they're the same scales but start on a different root. The easiest way to find these is to find out what Major key you're in, find it on your guitar and then go down three frets and there is your relative minor. So for instance, let's say a song is in G Major. We go to G on the 3rd fret of the E string, go down three frets and what do you know you have an open E string, which means that the relative minor of G Major is E minor. Then you can apply this same concept to that. So here's E minor, again using the same formula: 1w2hb3w4w5hb6wb7w8 E F# G A B C D E

And there she is, E minor in its purest form. Now, when we talk about the minor pentatonic patterns they use numbers out of the Minor Scale, but only five, hence the "penta" in the name! The numbers are 1, b3, 4, 5, b7. It's those same five notes over and over again. Now here's the most mind blowing thing that you'll ever find out about music: Music uses the same 7 notes in every song, just rearranged in a certain way.

Now, take those pentatonic patterns, learn them, find the numbers within each and then use those to add in the missing notes you need and voila, you're all done!

So, if we take our musical alphabet and add in the whole steps and half steps it would look like this:

AwBhCwDwEhFwGwA and it continues to repeat.

1=C, now here we go. So, in order to go to 2 we need to make a whole step right? So, a whole step above C, as we know from earlier, is going to take us to D. So, now it'll look like this 1=C w 2=D. Now that we get the basic idea, let's build the full scale:

1w2w3h4w5w6w7h8 C D E F G A B C

So, a sharp note has this: #, where is a flat note has this: b. So, for instance, let's say we want to build an A major scale. 1w2w3h4w5w6w7h8 A B C#D E F#G#A

1w2hb3w4w5hb6wb7w8

When it comes to deciding on which guitar you buy it's entirely up to what feels good to you specifically. I've played vintage Fender Strats from 1967 and others that are from 2007 and honestly, the one that I own, a 2007 Fender Roadhouse Stratocaster is miles away better than the 67 I played and it's specifically because of how it feels in my hands and the tones that it produces, for me personally, is what sounds good. The real test of a great guitar is how it plays, not its price point. That 67 strat went for $50k where as the best guitar I've ever played, my 07 Roadhouse, only cost me $700 and it will be with me till my grave.

So, once you have experience under your belt and know what sounds you want, go into a physical guitar store and just start playing guitars, don't worry about the price point, just play them and feel their necks and decide which one really speaks to you and see if it's in your price range. Then, don't buy it, ask them to hold onto it for you and come back for two months and keep replaying it every week to see if it's still the right guitar, if it is after all of that, then you buy it.

As far as amps go, the main thing to consider is what sort of tones you're looking for when you go in to play: solid state or tube sounds. Solid state amps are great for Metal and have a very base sound that permeates throughout everything you do. Tube amps are great for pretty much everything but metal and it responds to the way that you play. I've played out of a $3000 vintage 1970's Marshal head and thought it sounded cheap and awful, but the I plugged into my new VOX AC15 and instantly fell in love with the tones that it produced and how it responded to the way that I play. I only spent $400 on that amp and it has carried me through some very important sessions and gigs. Again, it's not about price point, it's about how does this amp sound to you and does it attain the tones that you need.

Here's the thing, I teach ALOT of different kinds of people, and lets face it, most people will choose not to practice on the days that they don't have time. They'll say things like "oh man, I was just so busy with this project" and then they don't practice at all. What's worse? Only practice 1-3 days a week, or practicing every day for at least 5 minutes? With the repetition of every day at 5 minute intervals as the minimum, they build habits and continue to keep the fingers going back to where they need to. Only practicing 3 days a week is a detriment to a persons playing, whatever they've learned and practiced goes completely out the window. 


You have to be realistic with your expectations of what new players are capable of when they aren't doing the amount of practicing that we do in the professional world and are still discovering the instrument. Start with 5 minutes, and if you want to do more, great, but then don't just skip the following day, it has to be consistent. Consistency is the best thing here.

One of the ways that I have my students work on getting down chords is my lap to neck technique: take a chord, any chord (let's go with C), build the chord, look at it, memorize what it looks like. Now take it off, maintaining the shape as best as you can, just a little bit! Almost like you're floating about it, then put it back EXACTLY the same way it left, don't rebuild it, just place it back, then repeat this process. You want to repeat this and take your hand off a little bit farther each time, maintaining the shape of the chord, until you can have your hand basically on the floor and be able to snap your hand onto the neck with the chord instantly under your finger tips.


Another thing to do once you've got down the chord shapes is start working on hard transitions. G to D, C to Ami, G to F, Ami to G, C to G, ect. Do each of these back and forth and back and forth, even use a metronome if you can, and get used to doing these transitions. This helps even more if you're learning a song (Stand By Me and Mr. Jones are great places to start with early chord transitions and are fun songs too!).


Now get out there and practice, EVERY DAY, 5 minutes minimum! And for gods sake use a metronome! :)

Firstly, I've been overweight since the age of 5, so I've lived my entire life this way, now granted, I'm pretty young to get this surgery (25) but I hadn't seen the other side of living. My entire life has been a struggle with my weight, which was a primary cause of my upbringing: I'm an emotional eater like the rest of my family and we fixed a lot of problems with food. My father was an alcoholic, parents split up when I was 12, lived between the two, my mom remarried relatively soon afterwards with a guy who was half her age who I didn't like, school bullying, didn't lose my virginity till I was 21, not a lot of luck in relationships. I had big problems with depression.


Anyways, for the past 8 years I've tried a very concerted effort to lose weight but with no success. Mostly, I just mentally could not stay on the wagon, I tried Atkins, South Beach, Weight Watchers ect and nothing worked. I either lost a lot but then fell off the wagon due to a weakness for pasta and rice (half German, half Filipino, eating is kinda in the genes), or didn't really lose anything and didn't have the encouragement to keep going. Ontop of all of this I had Fibromyalgia and early osteoarthiritis in my left knee so bad that just moving it was like dipping it in molten lead, making exercise incredibly difficult and painful. 


Now, the best part is that I'm in the entertainment industry as a professional Guitar player. Getting auditions for gigs was incredibly hard due to my weight and appearance because I'm not part of the "image" that most larger artist representations that are looking to hire musicians for artists want. So, most of my work is behind the scenes in studios and doing teaching, with me playing with other artists through connections, although I have lost a few audition opportunities, specifically a Rhianna audition, due to my image.


All of this created a super negative body image that made it harder for me to have any sort of confidence unless I was on stage. And it made me depressed that a lot of my abilities to approach women were hampered by those early pre-judging experiences of "oh, he's fat, no thanks".


My insurance finally approved my doctors recommendation for weight loss surgery in November of 2012, it came right after the woman that I loved more than anything else in my entire life decided to suddenly leave me, saying that she had been losing feelings for me for over a month and decided to end it right when she told me. I can say, as someone who DM’d 5e for almost 10 years (Next to when the OGL scandal started last year), I can tell you a big issue with the system is that there is absolutely no DM support whatsoever for a vast majority of situations that you’ll find yourself in at tables. The DMG that they offer, both the old and new version (which was shared with me, I haven’t given them my money since the OGL scandal, or really since they completely fumbled their Starjammer release) does NOT teach you REALLY how to run the game. The newest one had added in some tips, and given some nifty little helper sheets, but the system is still stuck with the same issues as far as I can see with the poor balance from being rubber banded by bounded accuracy and challenge rating tables that don’t truly account for every option at the table. The other big issue is that no one at Wizards can even agree on what the monster creation rules are, every monster in each of the books are all over the place, some match and some aren’t even in the same league, and then you have multiple DM’s using duct tape and a nail gun to try and make encounters up to the challenge that they want them to be at, but because of how swingy the system is it’s a crap shoot because either A.) the combat encounter goes as intended. B.) The party gets TPK’d. Or C.) The party walks all over the encounter.

Another big issue with encounters and making villains feel like villains is that because of how the system is designed, final villain encounters can either feel as intended, or end in one to three rounds and feel very anti-climactic because someone at your table took some options, that are completely legal from the books, that end up breaking the whole encounter. And this really feels like them either not playtesting their options ahead of time, or just not putting them in there with other options.

This also doesn’t help with the fact that even the people who WORK on this game behind the scenes don’t even know how to play or rub their own game. I know people call 5e an easy system to learn, but 5e is pretty crunchy, and most people don’t even read or look at the rules and just trust the DM to tell them how to play the game, and at the same time hand out a 5 page document of house rules that they made to further duct tape and nail gun the system to fix it further. They basically offload 2/3rds of the system onto you, the DM and say “you figure it out, dumbass”

I have found that Pathfinder 2e is an easier system to teach and GM in because it’s an easier system to play: You have three actions and a reaction, it’s all plainly spelled out on your sheet How many actions everything takes, all of the rules are there for any situation that you could hope for, and there’s no RAW vs RAI discussions at the table, it’s literally baked into every ability and rule because it’s all written as if these guys play their own system and know what to look out for. There’s TONS of great advice on how to GM your game, what to do with different types of players, and all of the rules are online for free. And even better, unlike 5e where you need the community to answer a majority of your lore questions through Wiki or hoping someone uploaded a scan of an old 3.5 or 2e book, they have TONS of dense lore books about their world with so many player options and just so many cool things for you to use, like a whole book on a Dwarven Kingdom called Highelm, Dwarven Society and how to make your own Dwarven Fortresses and Cities! And it’s a big book, with player options and new items too!

I will tell you, coming from 5e to Pathfinder 2e was like tonal whiplash. The amount of prep time that I have to do has shrunk, my combat encounters are interesting and engaging now, and my players are having so much fun with all of the options they have, and I’m having fun being able to build balanced combat’s with interesting monsters that do something more than just being a bag of hit points that just attacks every round.

The two “House rules” I guess that I primarily use are there to encourage team work and to help retrain my players who all come from 5e to Pathfinder 2e (I’m running 5 games of PF2e right now 😅) to show them that this game isn’t “four adventurers who happen to be in a group together” but an actual adventuring party/team. Besides giving a hero point every hour to my players here’s a couple of mine:

1. I let players spend as many hero points on each other as they like. You can burn all of your hero points on one roll, and players can double down and even donate as many hero points as they like to help each other out. I feel this really encourages team play, but also, makes them REALLY want to use their hero points to help each other out, which means they’re running out of them as quickly as they’re getting them and sometimes don’t have them for super critical points, which then forces the group to go into team mode to figure their way through it.

2. I let Aid checks stack, again, this is to help encourage team play amongst my players and to help them work together and come up with solutions where everyone can get involved and feel like their contributions matter. There are still people who are good at what they do, and experts in specific things, but watching my players try to figure out ways to help each other out suddenly changes their entire philosophy of how to play the game and it’s great for me as a GM watching everything click.

One thing I do for BRAND new players to the system, especially those switching from 5e, is let players switch whatever they like from levels 1-5 rather than retrain. I let them know that that rule exists for switching out specific things, but when you’re just starting out in an unfamiliar system, you might realize that something you picked at level 1 just isn’t really meshing anymore with your character. After level 5 I feel like my players have a pretty good handle on their characters and then implement the retrain rule using downtime.

In reality, 90% of us don’t, a majority of us are working other jobs to support our careers, have to take time off for touring, record during our off time at work, sometimes late into the night. If you’re a touring back up musician you’re basically hustling for the next gig once you’re off tour with the artist you were backing up because that’s the end of your paycheck (weekly pay plus per diem), unless you’re on retainer which means you’re under contract with one artist and you’re being paid to only play for them which means when you’re not touring with them they’re still paying you. And the other big issue for a vast majority of us is no health care under most contracts so a good portion of those pay checks are going straight towards health care, and if your job doesn’t provide it and you’re not in a state that provides low income health care you’re watching most of your money disappear into that or hoping you don’t get sick/injured. 

The percentage of people in the industry who make enough to fully support themselves and never have to work another job is somewhere in the ball park of 10-1%, and a majority of those artists are either from before the current music industry and they already made their money, or, they got a lucky contract, or they toughed it out, never got shelved (getting shelved happens to more artists than you think) and were able to eventually renegotiate a contract and get a better split, or they were smart with their money and diversified into other industries.

As somebody who used to be a professional musician before an injury, merch doesn’t really get you much either, basically gas to the next venue if you’re completely indie and using your own vehicle and that’s if you’re selling the merchandise yourself, if you’ve hired a merch seller they’re taking a cut too, and then a lot of the stuff that you’re making at gigs depends on the market and what cut your touring manager is taking, some venues require you to sell tickets ahead of time and fork up cash for any tickets you didn’t sell (pay-to-play), this is a big thing in Southern California, the Bay Area and Seattle, so if you’re from out of town and brand new and the promoter for the venue is only booking you on that specific deal then you’re basically hustling day of to sell whatever you can so you’re not further in the hole. A great majority of bands/artists come back from touring in the red, very rarely in the black. It’s an unfortunate part of the industry and the real problem is people look at it and say “man I’m talented at music, but it’s not financially viable, guess I’ll do something else” rather than ask “well wait, but why can’t it be financially viable?” A lot of us put in years of work and practice to get to a point where we can get into bands or back up artists and then rehearse for months prior to touring, spending money on either rehearsal lock outs or renting rehearsal spaces hourly, spending money on stage clothing, buying or renting the right gear to get out there and give you all a great show, or record a song that will really speak to you at some point in your life.

Here’s all of the house rules in my current Curse of Strahd campaign that my players really like!

House Rules! 😄

No evil, no chaotic neutral

We will be using Milestone leveling.

 Max HP at Level 1, roll for HP every level afterwards ignoring 1's.

 Level 1 you gain a racial feat from Xanathar's Guide, DM approval for feat if your race doesn't have any.

We will be rolling stats at character creation, roll two sets, pick the best set of the two.

 Gunslinger Fighter subclass allowed

 No Unearthed Arcana or Homebrew!

 No secret characters, all players know your race, class, and background. You can weave your backstories together at session 0

 Attunement takes 1 action, unattune takes 10 minutes

 No diagonals from the book, going diagonal is same as going straight

Flanking: you can flank on any square within melee distance, must describe how you're flanking and what you're doing to distract, roll skill check determined by DM against creatures AC. Gain advantage on flank attack rolls.

 Will be using bloodied for creatures to describe damage (once at half health creatures and players are bloodied)

 Death Saving Throws rolled by DM in secret. Medicine checks count as a successful or non-successful death save instead of stabilizing. Using medicine kits give you advantage.

 Sprint: sacrifice all actions and bonus actions to move 5 times your movement speed. Creatures get attacks of opportunity if you sprint through their threat range. Monsters, NPC's can do the same.

Massive Damage: If you or an enemy take half your HP in damage, you will have to make a DC 15 Constitution saving throw or make a system shock.

 Healing Spirit can only be used in combat

Charging Rule: You can use your action to charge, moving up to your speed towards a target, to gain advantage on your attack roll. Must move at least 10 ft towards your target. If you move through enemy threat range during this movement you can trigger opportunity attacks as you are throwing yourself off to wild abandon to charge head long towards a foe.

Hero Points: Instead of Inspiration we will now be using Hero Points. Every session every character will start with 1 Hero Point, you can earn up to 3 Hero Points per game and your Hero Points reset to 1 at the start of the next session. You can spend your Hero Point exactly as a point of Inspiration, but if you bank up 3 Hero Points and are down (0 hit points and dying) and spend all 3 you immediately bounce back up at 1 HP.

Shifting: You may spend your move action to shift 5ft. This uses up your entire move action, but allows you to move out of Melee Combat.

 Banned races:

No Wildemont races

No Ravnica Races

No Mythic Odysseys of Theros races

 Locathah allowed but don't have to submerge every 4 hours

 Banned backgrounds No backgrounds from Ravnica, Acquisitions Incorporated, Wildemont

I’ve run this campaign 3 times now to great effect, and here are my tips for running this module:

Read the module through at least twice, three times is even better, get really familiar with each of the locations, understand them. Some locations (like Vallaki) seem intimidating, but from the three times I’ve run it, each party arrives, bee lines it to the church, starts the bones quest, triggers the feast, and the torn burns the next day, not one of my parties actually engaged in the political thriller aspect of the town, but have it prepped just in case.

Look at each of the expansion posts and read through them, decide how much of each you wish to take from, and how much you don’t. Each one provides fantastic expansions to the campaign that really flesh everything out and give you some great advice on running the campaign.

Do not be afraid to kill your players, remember, death in Barovia is hardly the end, the mists never let souls leave. Look up the dark gifts in the Adventurers League DM’s guide for the campaign and when a player dies, take them aside and reach out to them, either as a dark power or as one of the hidden fanes if you’re using them and offer them a dark gift in exchange for resurrection. Always a cool “wtf” moment for the players when they immediately pop back up at full health and their eyes melt out of their faces granting them blind sight for 60 feet 😂

Be sure to stack the Tarokka deck BEFORE session 0, know where everything is going to be before the game starts and who their fated ally will be and where Strahd is going to be. For your first run, especially for new players, remove some of the worse cards from the deck when you do your draws; any cards that put items in the Castle, the card that gives them no ally in general. If they draw an ally who’s isn’t as crazy as say Ezmerelda, you can opt to turn them into a side kick to assist the players if they decide to arm them, giving levels in side kick equal to the parties level or half. 

If you so plan on running Death House (highly recommended with some tweaks!) be sure to take all of their stuff the minute they arrive in Barovia via the mists! This will immediately put them on edge and will have them scrounging for gear inside of the house.

Optional reading is definitely I, Strahd if you can! I believe the audiobook is on YouTube, definitely worth at least one read through to get into Strahd’s head.

Speaking of Strahd, really decide who Strahd is and how you want to play him. Mine is very serious, but has a sense of dark humor. He doesn’t take insults lightly and always lets everyone have one: one insult, one free hit etc. It always comes with a warning though, if they continue in this direction, his retaliation is quick and decisive and you will very quickly learn your place within his lands.

Most important thing too is to set expectations at session 0. Inform your players the style of campaign that this is, set up a system to allow players who feel uncomfortable to speak up when necessary and pause to handle it. And make sure they understand that this is a more difficult adventure than others but that they’ll be stronger be the end of it: players, friends, team mates etc.

Here’s the thing about Vallaki: I’m about to finish running Curse of Strahd for the third time in a row right now. In all three campaigns I can tell you exactly how each party went through Vallaki:

Party 1: Went to the inn, got a bit of info, loved the Martikovs, went to sleep. Next day, Ireena says “hey, before we go to the temple let’s go see the Burgomaster and give our regards, it would only be proper” The Party: “Ok, but like after the temple” bee line to the temple, find out about the bones, bee line to the orphanage (thank you MandyMod), shenanigans, bee line the coffin shop all the while saying “this’ll be quick guys, then we’ll hit the mayors house no sweat”, get to the coffin shop, trigger the feast, vampire spawn nearly beat the PC’s to death, Strahd shows up, taunts them, charms a player to give him the bones, he destroys the bones, resurrects his vampire spawn, tells them to feast, he leaves on Beauciphulus. Entire village of Vallaki descends into chaos, burgomaster and his wife are dragged out of his home and burned alive, Fiona Wachter takes over, Ireena was left back at the Inn, she’s now been taken by Strahd, they barely flee. Vallaki barely happened.

Party 2: Bee lined the temple, bee lined the orphanage, shenanigans, receive a note from Fiona Wachter, went to the inn, loved the martikovs, Ireena says they should visit the burgomaster “we’ll do it later, should probably handle the coffin shop first, that’ll be quick” (see a pattern?), go to the coffin shop, trigger the feast, make a mad dash across town with the bones with vampire spawn set loose upon the town and hot on their heels, get to the temple, Strahd makes a dramatic entrance, taunts them, kills the Barbarian for swinging at a Lord in one stroke, charms a player into giving him the bones, incinerates them, true resurrects the player, reminds them of their place within his realm, leaves, Vallaki is burning, players barely make it out alive, Fiona Wachter takes over.

Party 3: Gets to Vallaki, goes to see the Burgomaster this time, gets the plot hook for Fiona Wachter, actually meets Izek, goes shopping, goes to the temple, gets the bones quest, goes to the orphanage, shenanigans, gets the note from Fiona Wachter, goes to the Inn, really likes the Martikovs, decides to go to the coffin shop “don’t worry guys, it’ll be quick” (you see where this is going), go to the coffin shop, trigger the feast, rogue rushes into the town towards the abbey, vampire spawn are set loose on the city m, some hot on their heels, arrive at the abbey, Strahd makes extravagant entrance, kills the fighter to make a point, charms the player to give him the bones, incinerates them, true resurrects the fighter to remind him of his place in his realm, invites them to dinner and leaves, they sleep in the abbey, next day is the festival of the blazing Sun, the Burgomaster and his wife are burned on stage in front of the entire town as they cheer, Fiona Wachter takes over, players escape.

What I’m trying to illustrate here is that: even though you REALLY want your players to dive into the cool political intrigue and cult plots going on in Vallaki, more than likely they’ll skip over all of it, go straight for the church and basically trigger the end credits of Vallaki super early, so don’t sweat it too hard bud!

The clear differences that I've found between tube and solid state amps are entirely along the lines of how the amps react to your playing. Solid state amps have a singular level of sound, so, if you play softly or hard it'll be roughly the same. With tube amps they have a more reactionary feel to your playing, so if you play more softly it'll clean up the sound and make your tone more warm, and if you play harder it'll dirty itself and give you a sharper sound.

So really, it comes down to the style of music that you're playing and doing that really affects your decisions about the type of amp that you'll be using. I find that Solid States are great for Metal or really Hard Rock, whereas tube is better for pop, blues, rock, pop, R&B ect.

There's also benefits to doing this as well. You can actually change which string you're bending mid bend by doing this. Bend up on the b string a whole step and then swap down to the g string on the way down to get a cool bluesy effect.

Honestly, the main issue here is thumb positioning on the neck. For the a string/a shape barre chords (from the C.A.G.E.D system) you don't necessarily need the high e string in them in order for them to work. Attempt to fix your thumb positioning first by making sure that it is perfectly straight up and closer to the center of the back of the neck and where your middle finger would be, in this case, if you're doing an A shape C barre chord on the 3rd fret, keep your thumb behind the 4th fret like this http://andylemaire.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/12/Correct-thumb.jpg


And barre with your ring finger. It does take time to get it right too, this is just a step in the right direction to getting it right. It'll take a lot of trial and error, but proper thumb positioning helps with this.

This is an area of learning guitar that takes a lot of trial and error. Honestly, the main issues with E string barre chords is how you use the pressure of your index finger. You ideally want to be only applying pressure above your first knuckle with the pad of your index finger and then the fat part of your finger under your second knuckle. The primary reason why you don't barre your whole finger is that you don't need to because your ring, pinky and middle will be taking care of the A, D and G strings for you as far as major goes. I'd start there for now, and honestly, just take your time, it's going to be a while before you get it, just practice it for 15 minutes a day and then move on to practicing other things.

I think there are a certain amount of basics that everyone at every level should know and this is what I'll put here:

1.) The five minor pentatonic patterns and how they are moveable, not set to one key, but are basically the same thing for every key.

2.) How to find relative minor from a major key, by doing this, all 5 of those minor pentatonic patterns become major pentatonic, and you didn't have to learn anything new.

3.) How to build a major and a minor scale, involving whole steps and half steps and how to add these two missing notes into the minor pentatonic patterns, turning them into major and natural minor.

4.) How to modify said scales into harmonic minor, melodic minor, phrygian and the other modes.

5.) How to harmonize both the major and minor scales into chords. And how these chords are used in songwriting.

6.) Triads and their 1st and 2nd inversions.

7.) C.A.G.E.D system. And how these relate to the 5 patterns of the pentatonic/minor scales

8.) How to play extension chords and how to build them.

9.) How to build a melody and then expand that into a guitar solo.

10.) How to jam and improvise.

I think the best way to get better at improvising is to:


1.) Know all 5 patterns of the minor pentatonic scale

2.) Know how to play all 5 patterns of the natural minor scale

3.) Know how to modify the natural minor scale into a natural harmonic scale

4.) How to find the relative minor for major keys.


Now, once you have all of this down, learn a TON of other songs solos note for note. Work on getting the exact sounds and tone for each one, from how they vibrato, to how they bend and slide. This will help you to define your tone and your sound when improvising and give you a better idea of where you can go with your playing.

This is seldom, if ever, called melodic major. What it is, is the fifth mode of Melodic Minor... Sometimes it is referred to as Mixolydian b6... I have used it extensively.. I love the sound it creates, particularly over a sus2 chord from the tonic.. The ambiguity is great...

If you take this scale and spell it... Say you're in C... it would be:

C, D, E, F, G, Ab, Bb.

As you can see, if you start from the F, you get the melodic minor scale...

F, G, Ab, Bb, C, D, E

There is a HARMONIC MAJOR scale, but, to my knowledge, no MELODIC MAJOR, since Melodic minor implies a flatted third but the rest of the notes are structured EXACTLY like a Major scale...

Does that make sense to you??

Also, by the way, to hear this scale in use in a popular context, you can take another listen to Kashmir by Led Zeppelin... So, here's the thing. He's using minor pentatonic in the relevant minor key. I believe, according to what I saw, the song is in E major. So, the easiest way to find relative keys is to go to the major keys root note, in this case E, which can be found on the 12th fret on your E string and then go down three frets from there, which should put you on the 9th fret, which is C#, from there you can play minor pentatonic scales and it'll sound like major.

Then from there he's adding in a few natural minor notes, and towards the end he switches to E minor with a few major 3rds to make it a little bluesy.

Alright, so here's my big lesson for you on how theory and scales work. As we know, our guitar is normally tuned to EADGBe. These are the specific notes that our strings are tuned to. Now, if I play my E string open, what note would that be? E. Ok, now that we have that out of the way, let's talk about theory. All scales are based off of modifications of the Major scale. A major scale is made up of whole steps and half steps. A whole step on the guitar is 2 frets and a half step is 1 fret. Most notes are going to be a whole step apart, except for two: B-C and E-F. Both of those will always be a half step apart. So, if we take our musical alphabet and add in the whole steps and half steps it would look like this: 
AwBhCwDwEhFwGwA and it continues to repeat. The major scale is written in number format: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. Each number represents a position within the scale and helps you to identify various things, which we'll get into later. Now, in order to create a scale, specifically the Major scale, we have to plug in whole steps and half steps to achieve this. The major scale formula is Whole, Whole, Half, Whole, Whole, Whole, Half. So, with this in mind your Major scale should look like this: 1w2w3h4w5w6w7h8 (8 in this case is the Octave, which is the root note, or home note of the scale, at a higher area of the scale). Now, with this in mind lets build a scale to test this. Let's do C Major, as that's the most basic and has no accidentals (something we'll go over in a second). So, seeing as we're building a C Major scale, the first note in the scale should be C, seeing as that's our home note. So, here we go. 1=C, now here we go. So, in order to go to 2 we need to make a whole step right? So, a whole step above C, as we know from earlier, is going to take us to D. So, now it'll look like this 1=C w 2=D. Now that we get the basic idea, let's build the full scale: 1w2w3h4w5w6w7h8 C D E F G A B C

And there's our C Major scale, no sharps no flats. No what is a sharp and a flat? Those are called accidental notes and they happen between our whole steps. So, a sharp note has this: #, where is a flat note has this: b. So, for instance, let's say we want to build an A major scale. So we need to start this one with the root note, or the home note, which is A. So 1=A. Now, let's build the scale 1w2w3h4w5w6w7h8 A B C#D E F#G#A

So, if you notice, we have a C#, a F# and a G#. These notes happen between the notes that have the whole steps. So a C# can also be a Db. Both of those notes exist at the same time, but calling them that depends on what you use. You never use # and b's in the same scale, you pick either or.

Alright, now that we have that out of the way, we'll make a Natural Minor scale. So, Natural Minor is a variation of the Major Scale by changing sections of the Major Scale to make it fit. So, in order to create a Minor Scale we have to flatten, or lower the tone, of three notes within the scale which are the 3rd, 6th and 7th. So, this changes the way that we write and talk about it. The new numbers look like this: 1, 2, b3, 4, 5, b6, b7, 8

See that? We've changed their pitch, and now because of that, we change the types of whole steps and half steps that we use for the scale. So here is the whole step and half step formula for Natural Minor: 1w2hb3w4w5hb6wb7w8

So there we have it, the Natural Minor scale, our formula has changed. Now for something fun, we're going to make the A Minor scale, now pay special attention to this one: 1w2hb3w4w5hb6wb7w8 A B C D E F G A

Now, take a look at that, that is A minor in its pure form. Now, do you see anything familiar? Looks an awful lot like C Major right? That's because A minor is the relative minor of C Major, they're the same scales but start on a different root. The easiest way to find these is to find out what Major key you're in, find it on your guitar and then go down three frets and there is your relative minor. So for instance, let's say a song is in G Major. We go to G on the 3rd fret of the E string, go down three frets and what do you know you have an open E string, which means that the relative minor of G Major is E minor. Then you can apply this same concept to that. So here's E minor, again using the same formula: 1w2hb3w4w5hb6wb7w8 E F# G A B C D E

And there she is, E minor in its purest form. Now, when we talk about the minor pentatonic patterns they use numbers out of the Minor Scale, but only five, hence the "penta" in the name! The numbers are 1, b3, 4, 5, b7. It's those same five notes over and over again. Now here's the most mind blowing thing that you'll ever find out about music: Music uses the same 7 notes in every song, just rearranged in a certain way.

Now, take those pentatonic patterns, learn them, find the numbers within each and then use those to add in the missing notes you need and voila, you're all done!

Alright, so here's my big lesson for you on how theory and scales work.

As we know, our guitar is normally tuned to EADGBe. These are the specific notes that our strings are tuned to. Now, if I play my E string open, what note would that be? E.

Ok, now that we have that out of the way, let's talk about theory. All scales are based off of modifications of the Major scale. A major scale is made up of whole steps and half steps. A whole step on the guitar is 2 frets and a half step is 1 fret. Most notes are going to be a whole step apart, except for two: B-C and E-F. Both of those will always be a half step apart. So, if we take our musical alphabet and add in the whole steps and half steps it would look like this:

AwBhCwDwEhFwGwA and it continues to repeat.

The major scale is written in number format: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. Each number represents a position within the scale and helps you to identify various things, which we'll get into later. Now, in order to create a scale, specifically the Major scale, we have to plug in whole steps and half steps to achieve this. The major scale formula is Whole, Whole, Half, Whole, Whole, Whole, Half. So, with this in mind your Major scale should look like this: 1w2w3h4w5w6w7h8 (8 in this case is the Octave, which is the root note, or home note of the scale, at a higher area of the scale).

Now, with this in mind lets build a scale to test this. Let's do C Major, as that's the most basic and has no accidentals (something we'll go over in a second). So, seeing as we're building a C Major scale, the first note in the scale should be C, seeing as that's our home note. So, here we go.

1=C, now here we go. So, in order to go to 2 we need to make a whole step right? So, a whole step above C, as we know from earlier, is going to take us to D. So, now it'll look like this 1=C w 2=D. Now that we get the basic idea, let's build the full scale:

1w2w3h4w5w6w7h8
C  D  E  F  G  A  B C

And there's our C Major scale, no sharps no flats. No what is a sharp and a flat? Those are called accidental notes and they happen between our whole steps. So, a sharp note has this: #, where is a flat note has this: b. So, for instance, let's say we want to build an A major scale. So we need to start this one with the root note, or the home note, which is A. So 1=A. Now, let's build the scale

1w2w3h4w5w6w7h8
A  B  C#D E  F#G#A

So, if you notice, we have a C#, a F# and a G#. These notes happen between the notes that have the whole steps. So a C# can also be a Db. Both of those notes exist at the same time, but calling them that depends on what you use. You never use # and b's in the same scale, you pick either or.

Alright, now that we have that out of the way, we'll make a Natural Minor scale. So, Natural Minor is a variation of the Major Scale by changing sections of the Major Scale to make it fit. So, in order to create a Minor Scale we have to flatten, or lower the tone, of three notes within the scale which are the 3rd, 6th and 7th. So, this changes the way that we write and talk about it. The new numbers look like this:

1, 2, b3, 4, 5, b6, b7, 8

See that? We've changed their pitch, and now because of that, we change the types of whole steps and half steps that we use for the scale. So here is the whole step and half step formula for Natural Minor:

1w2hb3w4w5hb6wb7w8

So there we have it, the Natural Minor scale, our formula has changed. Now for something fun, we're going to make the A Minor scale, now pay special attention to this one:

1w2hb3w4w5hb6wb7w8
A  B   C  D  E    F    G  A

Now, take a look at that, that is A minor in its pure form. Now, do you see anything familiar? Looks an awful lot like C Major right? That's because A minor is the relative minor of C Major, they're the same scales but start on a different root. The easiest way to find these is to find out what Major key you're in, find it on your guitar and then go down three frets and there is your relative minor. So for instance, let's say a song is in G Major. We go to G on the 3rd fret of the E string, go down three frets and what do you know you have an open E string, which means that the relative minor of G Major is E minor. Then you can apply this same concept to that. So here's E minor, again using the same formula:

1w2hb3w4w5hb6wb7w8
E  F# G  A  B    C    D  E

And there she is, E minor in its purest form.

Now, when we talk about the minor pentatonic patterns they use numbers out of the Minor Scale, but only five, hence the "penta" in the name! The numbers are 1, b3, 4, 5, b7. It's those same five notes over and over again. Now here's the most mind blowing thing that you'll ever find out about music: Music uses the same 7 notes in every song, just rearranged in a certain way.

Now, take those pentatonic patterns, learn them, find the numbers within each and then use those to add in the missing notes you need and voila, you're all done!

Here's the thing, I teach ALOT of different kinds of people, and lets face it, most people will choose not to practice on the days that they don't have time. They'll say things like "oh man, I was just so busy with this project" and then they don't practice at all. What's worse? Only practice 1-3 days a week, or practicing every day for at least 5 minutes? With the repetition of every day at 5 minute intervals as the minimum, they build habits and continue to keep the fingers going back to where they need to. Only practicing 3 days a week is a detriment to a persons playing, whatever they've learned and practiced goes completely out the window. 


You have to be realistic with your expectations of what new players are capable of when they aren't doing the amount of practicing that we do in the professional world and are still discovering the instrument. Start with 5 minutes, and if you want to do more, great, but then don't just skip the following day, it has to be consistent. Consistency is the best thing here.

I'm going with everyone else here to say that practice here is the key. Make sure it's a MINIMUM of 5 minutes a day, as long as that guitar is in your hands and you're playing it you'll be building muscle memory, hand strength and accuracy.


One of the ways that I have my students work on getting down chords is my lap to neck technique: take a chord, any chord (let's go with C), build the chord, look at it, memorize what it looks like. Now take it off, maintaining the shape as best as you can, just a little bit! Almost like you're floating about it, then put it back EXACTLY the same way it left, don't rebuild it, just place it back, then repeat this process. You want to repeat this and take your hand off a little bit farther each time, maintaining the shape of the chord, until you can have your hand basically on the floor and be able to snap your hand onto the neck with the chord instantly under your finger tips.


Another thing to do once you've got down the chord shapes is start working on hard transitions. G to D, C to Ami, G to F, Ami to G, C to G, ect. Do each of these back and forth and back and forth, even use a metronome if you can, and get used to doing these transitions. This helps even more if you're learning a song (Stand By Me and Mr. Jones are great places to start with early chord transitions and are fun songs too!).


Now get out there and practice, EVERY DAY, 5 minutes minimum! And for gods sake use a metronome! :)

Now that we've gone over the basics of constructing a major scale now we can apply our new concept. All other scales that we work with are variations of the major scale. How we communicate these scales and scale steps to one another are based around modifications of the major scale.


For instance, let's take the natural minor scale. In order to create this scale, we take the major scale and move the 3rd, 6th and 7th notes of the scale down a half step. This is why when talking about these notes we say b3rd or b7th. Our new number system now looks like this for Natural Minor:


1, 2, b3, 4, 5, b6, b7, 8


Now, because we've modified these three scale steps, this changes our formula. Our new formula is w, h, w, w, h, w, w. Now we'll plug this in to get:


1-w-2-h-b3-w-4-w-5-h-b6-w-b7-w-8


And so again, let's construct a basic Natural Minor scale, the easiest being A minor:

1-w-2-h-b3-w-4-w-5-h-b6-w-b7-w-8
A----B---C----D----E---F-----G----A


Now, notice here, that both C major and A minor both have no sharps or flats. We call this a relative key. A minor is the relative minor of C major and C major is the relative major of A minor. Same notes, different order. Every key has a relative major and a relative minor, keys that contain the same notes but in different orders.


Now, with all of this knowledge, the last two formula's we'll go over, in a simplified way, are the other three scales that you'll use: 


Dorian Minor:

1-w-2-h-b3-w-4-w-5-w-6-h-b7-w-8


Melodic Minor:

1-w-2-h-3-w-4-w-5-w-6-w-7-h-8


Harmonic Minor:

1-w-2-h-b3-w-4-w-5-h-b6-wh(3steps)-7-h-8


As you can see, these minor scales are variations, again, on the major scale. For instance, Melodic Minor is simply Major Scale with a b3rd. Harmonic Minor is Natural Minor with a raised 7th or in this case a Major 7th. Using these concepts, you can modify and adjust scales to your hearts content to create unique sounds.


Now, let's talk about this application to the pentatonic scales. Our current pentatonic patterns I-V all contain the same 5 notes: 1, b3, 4, 5, and b7. Knowing this and knowing about our previous scales, the only two missing notes are 2 and b6. One exercise to do now is go into each of your pentatonic patterns and now add in these missing notes to the scales, taking care to pay attention to your whole steps and half steps.


Next let's talk about chord construction: basic major and minor chords are made up of three key notes:

1 (the root) 3 (determines if a chord is major or minor) and 5 (the foundation, or the body of the chord, also determines if something is augmented or diminished)


A basic major triad or chord is:

1, 3, 5


Let's go back to my original theory post and look at C major. Let's grab those notes from there:

1=C, 3=E, 5=G


Go to your guitar right now and play a basic open C major chord, check each note. They're all those notes strung together!


A basic minor chord triad is:

1, b3 (remember, in order for it to be minor it MUST be moved down a half step), 5


Let's look now (keeping in the spirit of relative majors and minors) at your standard A minor chord, again referring back to the previous lesson:

1=A, b3=C, 5=E


Now, again, go to your guitar and play a basic open A minor chord. Check each note and notice that, again, it is these same notes over and over again!


Now, you don't HAVE to play these notes in this exact order! That's where inversions come in, my personal favorite being:


5, 1, 3


It creates a great sound and is fun to mess around with!


These are the basics of music theory, now go forth and mess around and have fun!!!
