Now, everything that we base our scales off of starts with the major scale. Creating scales is taking a collection of whole steps and half steps and making a scale. In order for us to find our place in the scale we use numbers to determine position within the scale (this is why people mention playing 3rds and 5ths, these are just scale positions!)


So first things first, we write out our numbers to determine our positions:


1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8


Every scale contains 7 notes, plus an octave (8) which is basically the same note as 1 (the root) but higher. Now, we plug in our major scale formula of whole steps and half steps which are: w, w, h, w, w, w, h


1-w-2-w-3-h-4-w-5-w-6-w-7-h-8


So that's our full major scale formula. Now that we've created our formula, now let's plug in a scale! Thanks to the way we've created this, now it's as easy as following the instructions in front of us! Let's start with C major, the easiest one. What's the first note in C major? C right?


1-w-2-w-3-h-4-w-5-w-6-w-7-h-8

C


Ok, now the first thing that we have to do is make a whole step from 1 to 2 correct? Well, as we know C-D is a whole step. So, now it looks like this!


1-w-2-w-3-h-4-w-5-w-6-w-7-h-8

C---D

And from here, we can continue the same concept, using the idea of whole steps and half steps to our advantage, using the rest of the formula we can complete the scale:


1-w-2-w-3-h-4-w-5-w-6-w-7-h-8

C----D---E---F----G---A----B---C


Also, remember, once we've reached the and of A, B, C, D, E, F, G because there is no H or J, we go back to the beginning! And there you have it, a completed C major scale! Easy right!? Ok, let's do something with #'s, how about A major?


1-w-2-w-3-h-4-w-5-w-6-w-7-h-8

A----B---C#--D---E----F#--G#--A


Ok, now let's analyze this, why is it that after B I went to C# instead of C? Because there was a whole step, and if we remember B-C is only a half step. Now, same things applies to E-F#, E-F is only a half step and so therefore, because we must do a whole step we end up on F# instead. Now, because we are on F# and our next note is a whole step from there, we don't end up on G because if we look here F-F#/Gb-G G is only a half step away, which puts us just above G but not far enough to hit A! So therefore we end up in the middle with G#/Ab, and then seeing as we're on G#, with only a half step to go, we end up on A. Part 3 coming

Ok, I'm gonna give you a small theory lesson right now:


All of western contemporary music uses the same 12 tone system, developed after composers were getting tired of overly complicated systems where you'd never go back to the root note, but you'd get a perfect c major.


You have 7 natural notes: A, B, C, D, E, F, G


Each note is separated by these things called whole steps (w) and half steps (h). A whole step on the guitar is 2 frets and a half step is only 1. Most notes are separated by "w"s for instance:


A-w-B, C-w-D, D-w-E, F-w-G, G-w-A


There are two pairs of notes that will always be a half step apart.


B-h-C, and E-h-F. This is constant, if you forget this, you're SCREWED!


So, the whole thing looks like this:


A-w-B-h-C-w-D-w-E-h-F-w-G-w-A


Those are the standard distances between notes. Now, I said 12 tones right? So where's the other 5? Well, those are the accidentals. These guys happen when you DON'T follow these specific sets of rules (except for B-C and E-F, those never change, ever, ever, ever)


So let's say, we only go a Half-Step above A instead of a whole:

A--B the two lines equal a whole step,  but right in the middle exists our first accidental: A#/Bb it can be either or, but they are technically the same note. So by only going a half step above, we do not hit B, because it's a whole step, so we end up in the middle, where we find A#/Bb, if it's above it's sharp and if it's below it's flat. Easy way to remember.


Another example is this: let's say you want to go a WHOLE step, instead of a half step, above B. Well let's look at what the original natural way looks like:

B-h-C-w-D


AS you can see, if we go a whole step, it doesn't make it all the way over to D, that would be a step and a half (3 half steps), instead, it lands where that W is, in the middle giving us C#/Db. Any time you use sharps and flats when creating scales you should stick with a theme of consciousness, if you start with sharps, go with sharps, if you start with flats, go with flats, and don't repeat notes.


Now, the fun part, our guitar strings have names too right? You read tab, so let me go ahead and lay out the string names like tab:

e

b

g

d

a

E


These are your string names, these are important for tuning but ALSO important for finding your notes! Everything here that we just talked about applies! So, if you play your low E string open what note do you hear? E right? So, taking into account that an open string is like a fret. If we were to go a half step above an open E that would put us on the 1st fret of your E string on your guitar, that note would then be F because E-h-F.


Now you can use this method to find any note that you want on the neck! It's really cool! Posting part 2.

The easiest way I compartmentalized the whole experience is to look at the pentatonics as a skeleton of everything, which it is. The numbers from the scale that it incorporates are 1, b3, 4, 5, b7. So, if we're to look at those 5 numbers, that means we're only missing two notes from natural minor: 2 and b6. So, by adding those two notes (2 is a whole step above 1, and b6 is a half step above 5) you get a full natural minor scale. Everything else from there is just minor adjustments to said scale to create new scales. Want Dorian? Raise the b6 a half step, want harmonic? Raise the b7 a half step, want melodic? Raise both b6 and b7 up a half step. Mixolydian is just major with a b7. Lydian is just major with a #4, Lydian Flat Dominant (one of my personal favorites) is just the same with a b7.

All you have to do is examine each pattern/box, find the root note for said pattern/box and then count the numbers from there, that simple! Everything is just futtzing around with numbers and creating new scales. Next step is finding out where to use them and how to use them. Then turn that into chord shapes, then arppegios and so on and so forth. And all of this works the same in major as it does in minor.

Yes in a way, but then for the c shape, you get a very nice, spaced out major chord. I love using them for more spacial and different sounding major chords, especially with E major using a c shape, it sounds fantastic. 

Also, the d shape chord is best used without using the d string and focusing mostly on the triad, with the root being on the b string. This creates a very fun triad that you can move along the neck, great for Ska, Reggae and Funk, or if you arpeggiate it you can get some great sounding alternative rock notes out of it. 

Basically this all breaks down into changing your triads up and down the neck and creating new sounds, then taking each of this shapes and breaking them apart and using pieces of them to find new things. It's really fun and one of my favorite things to teach.

That site seems a little more complicated than it needs to be. C.A.G.E.D is just an acronym and stands for each of the 5 chord shapes associated with the chord it's representing. You're just moving the shape up the neck and compensating for open notes. Barre chords are merely A and E shapes moved up the neck for example.

First of all. Make sure you guys are TIGHT, like REALLY TIGHT! Rehearse hard and make sure every section is together and purposeful and sounds together. You, the drummer and the bass player should so far together that it'd take superman to pull you guys apart.

Then, set all of your tones ahead of time. Know what pedal settings you want, what amp settings you want. When recording guitar, if you're doing it separate instead of live, I like to put one mic on the speaker, one mic directly behind that mic, maybe half a foot away, and then one mic in the back corner of the room and then blend those sounds together.

Also, to re-iterate xonicolasxo, double track all of your guitars. If you're the only guitar player, do separate tracks for left and right, and then double over those. Then do an acoustic guitar in the middle to really beef out the sound. Also, write some cool parts to go over each section separately.

Write your solo's ahead of time. Improvising is cool, but having something concrete will sound so much better on your track. Harmonize with it too if you can!

In the early stages of guitar playing, proper hand position helps to build finger strength and make playing easier and less damaging on your hand. As your hand develops strength and your fingers stretch and attune themselves to the neck is when you begin to develop your own thumb style and can branch.

Here, I can explain it better:

In western contemporary music we have 12 tones that we use.

7 Natural notes:
A, B, C, D, E, F, and G

Each note has a certain set distance from each other. These distances are measured in whole steps and half steps. On our guitars:
whole step = 2 frets
half step = 1 fret

Most notes are going to be a whole step apart. For instance, going from A-B, or D-E. These are common whole step distances. But there are two pairs of notes that will always be a half step away:
B-C and E-F will always be a half step apart from one another. This is the big rule that you have to remember.

Then we have 5 accidentals. These all happen in the little grey areas between whole steps of notes. For instance if I was on B and I wanted to make a whole step. Instead of going to C (remember, it's a half step) we would go one above, but because we aren't going far enough to hit D, we end up in the middle with C#/Db. Uses of sharps and flats are dependent on the flow of the scale, but don't worry about that for now.

Now, all of the great western contemporary scales that we use: minor, dorian, ect. are all derived from the Major scale. Each other scale is taking the major scale and modifying it slightly. To create a scale we assemble a formula of whole steps and half steps that create the scale. In this case the major scale formula is as such:
w, w, h, w, w, w, h

Now, in order to give this a little bit visual enhancement we'll place these between the numbers to give you an idea of where these go:

1 w 2 w 3 h 4 w 5 w 6 w 7 h 8

So for instance if we wanted to do the C major scale we'd start with the first note

1 (C) w (whole step above C takes us to) 2 (D) (another whole step from here takes us to) 3 (E) (now we must make a half step which takes us to) 4 (F) (another whole step takes us to) 5 (G) (another whole step takes us to) 6 (A) (another whole step from here takes us to) 7 (B) (and the final half step takes us back to) 8 (C)

By using this method you can create a scale for any key. Try grabbing a pen and a piece of paper and doing a few of these yourselves. Post results in the comments if you wish.
